```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 2 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Vector Spaces</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">2.2</span> Vector Space, Dual Space, and Tensor Space</h1></header>
<p>We now formally define the concept of an <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector space, along with the related notions of linear maps, isomorphisms, and the dual vector space (rows 3 and 4 of Figure <a class="dg-xref" href="../introduction/roadmaps.html#fig_vector_spaces_roadmap" data-kind="figure" data-label="fig_vector_spaces_roadmap">1.2</a>). Note that, at this stage, the definitions are purely algebraic and do not rely on any choice of basis. See appendices <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-vector-space.html#subsection_appendix_Check_for_Vector_Space_Properties" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_appendix_Check_for_Vector_Space_Properties">C.1.1</a> &amp; <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-vector-space.html#subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_objects" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_objects">C.1.2</a> for concrete examples illustrating these definitions employing polynomials.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>An <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange"><span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector space</span> is the triplet <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span> equipped with the Field <span class="math inline">\((\mathbb{R}, +, \cdot)\)</span>. The doublet <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus)\)</span> forms an Abelian group, and the s-multiplication operator <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange"><span class="math inline">\(\odot: \mathbb{R} \times V \to V\)</span></span> satisfies (considering <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V\)</span>, elements of the vector space, known as <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">vectors</span>, and <span class="math inline">\(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>):</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Associativity (w.r.t <span class="math inline">\(\cdot, \odot\)</span>): <span class="math inline">\((\alpha \cdot \beta) \odot \mathcal{X} = \alpha \odot (\beta \odot \mathcal{X})\)</span>,</p></li>
<li><p>Distributive 1: <span class="math inline">\((\alpha + \beta) \odot \mathcal{X} = (\alpha \odot \mathcal{X}) \oplus (\beta \odot \mathcal{X})\)</span>,</p></li>
<li><p>Distributive 2: <span class="math inline">\(\alpha \odot (\mathcal{X} \oplus \mathcal{Y}) = (\alpha \odot \mathcal{X}) \oplus (\alpha \odot \mathcal{Y})\)</span>,</p></li>
<li><p>Unitarity / Neutral element / Identity (w.r.t <span class="math inline">\(\odot\)</span>): <span class="math inline">\(\exists 1 \in \mathbb{R}\)</span> such that <span class="math inline">\(1 \odot \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X} \odot 1 = \mathcal{X}\)</span>.</p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\)</span> be vector spaces. The map <span class="math inline">\(\phi : V \to W\)</span> is <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">linear</span> (w.r.t. the vector spaces we have defined, also denoted as <span class="math inline">\(\phi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} W\)</span>) <span class="math inline">\(\iff \forall \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in V; \, \forall \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><span class="math inline">\( \phi(\mathcal{X} \oplus_V \mathcal{Y}) = \phi(\mathcal{X}) \oplus_W \phi(\mathcal{Y}) \)</span>, and</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\( \phi(\alpha \odot_V \mathcal{X}) = \alpha \odot_W \phi(\mathcal{X}) \)</span>.</p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p>Given two <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector spaces <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\)</span>, a map <span class="math inline">\(\phi : V \longrightarrow W\)</span> is a (vector space) <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">isomorphism</span> if it is linear and bijective, hence invertible. If such a map exists, we say that the vector spaces <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span> are <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">isomorphic</span>, and we write <span class="math inline">\(V \cong W\)</span>. Intuitively, this means that <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span> have the same structure as vector spaces.</p></li>
<li><p>The Vector Space of <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">Homomorphisms</span> between two vector spaces <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus_V, \odot_V)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((W, \oplus_W, \odot_W)\)</span> is the triplet conformed by the set <span class="math inline">\(\text{Hom}(V, W) := \{ \phi, \varphi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} W \}\)</span>, and the operations:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \textbf{Addition } \oplus_H: \\[6pt]
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \oplus_H : \text{Hom}(V, W) \times \text{Hom}(V, W) &amp;\longrightarrow \text{Hom}(V, W) \\
                        (\phi, \varphi) &amp;\longmapsto \phi \oplus_H \varphi
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } (\phi \oplus_H \varphi)(v) := \phi(v) \oplus_W \varphi(v).
                \end{array}
                \quad
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \textbf{s-multiplication } \odot_H: \\[6pt]
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \odot_H : \mathbb{R} \times \text{Hom}(V, W) &amp;\longrightarrow \text{Hom}(V, W) \\
                        (\lambda, \phi)                              &amp;\longmapsto \lambda \odot_H \phi
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } (\lambda \odot_H \phi)(v) := \lambda \odot_W \phi(v).
                \end{array}
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Given a vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span>, we define its <span class="dg-term dg-term-red">Dual Vector Space</span> as <span class="math inline">\((V^* , \oplus^*, \odot^*)\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(V^* := \text{Hom}(V, \mathbb{R}) := \{ \phi : V \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{R} \}\)</span>, and the addition and s-multiplication operators, <span class="math inline">\(\oplus^*\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\odot^*\)</span>, following the associatted homomorphic definitions above. We will denote with <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}\)</span> elements of the dual vector space <span class="math inline">\(V^*\)</span> known as <span class="dg-term dg-term-red">covectors</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Given a vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span> and its dual vector space <span class="math inline">\((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\)</span>, we define the <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown"><span class="math inline">\((r,s)\)</span>-tensor space</span> as the triplet <span class="math inline">\(\left( {T}^{(r,s)}, \oplus_T, \odot_T \right)\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\({T}^{(r,s)}\)</span> is the set of all maps of the form<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-2" id="fnref-2" aria-label="Footnote 2">2</a></sup> <sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3" aria-label="Footnote 3">3</a></sup>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            T \colon
            \underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{r \text{-times}}
            \times
            \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{s \text{-times}}
            &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\
            \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right)
            &amp;\longmapsto
            T \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right),
        \end{align*}</span>  with the property that <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span> is <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">multilinear</span>, i.e., it is <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-linear with respect to each of its <span class="math inline">\(r + s\)</span> slots independently. The multilinearity condition explicitly reads:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p>For any covector slot <span class="math inline">\(i \in \{1, \dots, r\}\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\[
                    \begin{aligned}
                        T \left( \dots,\; \alpha \odot^* \mathsf{X}^{(i)} \oplus^* \mathsf{Y}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right) =
                        \alpha \cdot T \left( \dots,\; \mathsf{X}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right)
                        + T \left( \dots,\; \mathsf{Y}^{(i)},\; \dots;\; \dots \right),
                    \end{aligned}
                \]</span>  for any <span class="math inline">\(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\)</span> and any <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}, \mathsf{Y}^{(i)} \in V^*\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Similarly, for any vector slot <span class="math inline">\(j \in \{1, \dots, s\}\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\[
                    \begin{aligned}
                        T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \alpha \odot \mathcal{X}^{(j)} \oplus \mathcal{Y}^{(j)},\; \dots \right) =
                        \alpha \cdot T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \mathcal{X}^{(j)},\; \dots \right)
                        + T \left( \dots;\; \dots,\; \mathcal{Y}^{(j)},\; \dots \right),
                    \end{aligned}
                \]</span>  for any <span class="math inline">\(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\)</span> and any <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}, \mathcal{Y}^{(j)} \in V\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The addition <span class="math inline">\(\oplus_T\)</span> and the s-multiplication <span class="math inline">\(\odot_T\)</span> in the <span class="math inline">\((r,s)\)</span>-tensor space <span class="math inline">\(\left( {T}^{(r,s)}, \oplus_T, \odot_T \right)\)</span> are the defined as:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \oplus_T : {T}^{(r,s)} \times {T}^{(r,s)} &amp;\longrightarrow {T}^{(r,s)} \\
                        (T_1, T_2) &amp;\longmapsto T_1 \oplus_T T_2
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } (T_1 \oplus_T T_2)(\dots) := T_1(\dots) + T_2(\dots).
                \end{array}
                \quad
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \odot_T : \mathbb{R} \times {T}^{(r,s)} &amp;\longrightarrow {T}^{(r,s)} \\
                        (\alpha, T)                             &amp;\longmapsto \alpha \odot_T T
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } (\alpha \odot_T T)(\dots) := \alpha \cdot T(\dots).
                \end{array}
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Given two <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector spaces <span class="math inline">\(\left( V, \oplus_V, \odot_V \right)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left( W, \oplus_W, \odot_W \right)\)</span>, we define their <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">tensor product</span> as the <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>-vector space <span class="math inline">\(\left( V \otimes W, \oplus_\otimes, \odot_\otimes \right)\)</span>, whose elements are finite sums <span class="math inline">\(\tau = \sum_{k} \alpha_k \, (v_k \otimes w_k)\)</span> of simple tensors <span class="math inline">\(v_k \otimes w_k\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>, and whose operations act term by term:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \textbf{Addition} \; \oplus_\otimes: \\[6pt]
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \oplus_\otimes : (V \otimes W) \times (V \otimes W)
                        &amp;\longrightarrow V \otimes W \\[2pt]
                        (\tau_1,\; \tau_2) &amp;\longmapsto \tau_1 \oplus_\otimes \tau_2
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } \displaystyle\sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k) \oplus_\otimes \sum_{l} \beta_l (v'_l \otimes w'_l)
                    := \sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k) + \sum_{l} \beta_l (v'_l \otimes w'_l).
                \end{array}
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span>  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                &amp;\begin{array}{c}
                    \textbf{s-multiplication} \; \odot_\otimes: \\[6pt]
                    \begin{aligned}
                        \odot_\otimes : \mathbb{R} \times (V \otimes W)
                        &amp;\longrightarrow V \otimes W \\[2pt]
                        (\alpha,\; \tau) &amp;\longmapsto \alpha \odot_\otimes \tau
                    \end{aligned} \\[6pt]
                    \text{with } \alpha \odot_\otimes \displaystyle\sum_{k} \alpha_k (v_k \otimes w_k)
                    := \sum_{k} (\alpha \cdot \alpha_k) (v_k \otimes w_k).
                \end{array}
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Two such sums are regarded as the same element whenever one can be turned into the other using the <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">bilinearity</span> relations:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                (v_1 \oplus_V v_2) \otimes w
                &amp;= (v_1 \otimes w) \oplus_\otimes (v_2 \otimes w), \\[4pt]
                v \otimes (w_1 \oplus_W w_2)
                &amp;= (v \otimes w_1) \oplus_\otimes (v \otimes w_2), \\[4pt]
                (\alpha \odot_V v) \otimes w
                &amp;= \alpha \odot_\otimes (v \otimes w)
                = v \otimes (\alpha \odot_W w).
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span>  The general elements of <span class="math inline">\(V \otimes W\)</span> are finite linear combinations:  <span class="math display">\[
            \sum_{k} \alpha_k \odot_\otimes (v_k \otimes w_k), \quad \alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}.
        \]</span>  The tensor product formalizes the concept of <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">bilinearity</span> itself into a linear structure. This provides the algebraic backbone that generalizes naturally to <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">multilinearity</span>, which underlies the formal definition of tensors as higher-order linear maps. The tensor product enjoys the following structural properties:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p>Universal Property: For any bilinear map, <span class="math inline">\(B : V \times W \longrightarrow Z\)</span>, into a vector space <span class="math inline">\(Z\)</span>, there exists a unique linear map <span class="math inline">\(\widetilde{B} : V \otimes W \longrightarrow Z\)</span> such that <span class="math inline">\(\widetilde{B} (v \otimes w) = B(v, w)\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(v \in V\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(w \in W\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Dimension Formula: If <span class="math inline">\(\dim V = m\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\dim W = n\)</span>, then <span class="math inline">\(\dim ( V \otimes W ) = m \cdot n\)</span>. A basis is given by the set of tensor products of basis elements:  <span class="math display">\[
                    \{ \hat{x}_i \otimes \hat{y}_j \mid i=1,\dots,m;\; j=1,\dots,n \},
                \]</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{x}_i\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{y}_j\}\)</span> are bases of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(W\)</span>, respectively.</p></li>
<li><p>Associativity: Tensor products are associative up to canonical isomorphism: <span class="math inline">\((V_1 \otimes V_2) \otimes V_3 \cong V_1 \otimes (V_2 \otimes V_3)\)</span>. It is customary to omit parentheses and write unambiguously: <span class="math inline">\(V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Distributivity over Direct Sums: Tensor products distribute over direct sums:  <span class="math display">\[
                    (V_1 \oplus_V V_2) \otimes W
                    \cong
                    (V_1 \otimes W) \oplus_\otimes (V_2 \otimes W).
                \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Duality Relation: There is a canonical isomorphism <span class="math inline">\(\text{Hom}(V \otimes W, \mathbb{R}) \cong \text{Bilin}(V \times W, \mathbb{R})\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(\text{Bilin}(V \times W, \mathbb{R})\)</span> denotes the space of bilinear maps from <span class="math inline">\(V \times W\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>An equivalent way to define an <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown"><span class="math inline">\((r,s)\)</span>-tensor</span> on a finite-dimensional vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span> is as an element of the <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">tensor product space</span>  <span class="math display">\[
            T^{(r,s)} \cong \underbrace{V \otimes \dots \otimes V}_{r\text{-times}}
            \otimes
            \underbrace{V^* \otimes \dots \otimes V^*}_{s\text{-times}}.
        \]</span>  Note the order of the factors: the <span class="math inline">\(r\)</span> <em>covector</em> slots of the multilinear map are matched by <span class="math inline">\(r\)</span> copies of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>, and the <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> <em>vector</em> slots by <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> copies of <span class="math inline">\(V^*\)</span>. This is because a vector <span class="math inline">\(v \in V\)</span> can eat covectors through the canonical identification <span class="math inline">\(V \cong (V^*)^*\)</span> discussed in the next item, <span class="math inline">\(v(\mathsf{X}) \coloneqq \mathsf{X}(v)\)</span>, while a covector eats vectors directly. Accordingly, a simple tensor with <span class="math inline">\(v_1, \dots, v_r \in V\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{v}^1, \dots, \mathsf{v}^s \in V^*\)</span> acts slot by slot,  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( v_1 \otimes \dots \otimes v_r \otimes \mathsf{v}^1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathsf{v}^s \right)
            \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right)
            \coloneqq
            \mathsf{X}^{(1)}(v_1) \cdots \mathsf{X}^{(r)}(v_r) \cdot
            \mathsf{v}^1\big(\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\big) \cdots \mathsf{v}^s\big(\mathcal{X}^{(s)}\big),
        \]</span>  which is manifestly multilinear, and a general element of the tensor product space acts by extending this rule linearly (which is well defined by the universal property). The resulting linear map from the tensor product space to the space of multilinear maps defined above is an isomorphism when <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> is finite-dimensional: both spaces have dimension <span class="math inline">\(d^{\,r+s}\)</span> and, as shown below, the images of simple tensors of basis elements span the space of multilinear maps. This is the precise sense in which both definitions are equivalent, and the reason for the symbol <span class="math inline">\(\cong\)</span>.</p>
<p>In this definition, tensors are no longer described as multilinear maps, but rather as elements of a vector space constructed through tensor products. Both perspectives are fully equivalent: the first is often more intuitive for understanding the action of tensors, while the second is more algebraic and convenient for computations, particularly in component form.</p></li>
<li><p>We can also think of tensors as follows: Given a <span class="math inline">\((1,1)\)</span>-tensor  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            T :
            V^* \times V
            &amp;\;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}}\; \mathbb{R}\\
            \left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right)
            &amp;\longmapsto
            T\left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right).
        \end{align*}</span>  We can associate to any such tensor a linear map  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \varphi_T :V
            &amp;\;\xlongrightarrow{\sim}\; V\\
            \mathcal{X} &amp;\longmapsto \varphi_T(\mathcal{X}) \coloneqq T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}),
        \end{align*}</span>  where the dot “<span class="math inline">\(\cdot\)</span>” indicates that the first slot is left open. More explicitly, the map  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}) :
            V^*
            &amp;\;\xlongrightarrow{\sim}\; \mathbb{R}\\
            \mathsf{X} &amp;\longmapsto T\left( \mathsf{X}, \mathcal{X} \right),
        \end{align*}</span>  is a linear map that can eat a covector <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\)</span> and return a real number. Hence, <span class="math inline">\(T(\cdot, \mathcal{X}) \in (V^*)^*\)</span>, that is, the dual of <span class="math inline">\(V^*\)</span>. In finite-dimensional vector spaces, there exists a canonical isomorphism <span class="math inline">\((V^*)^* \cong V\)</span> which identifies <span class="math inline">\((V^*)^*\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span> itself <sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup>. Therefore, <span class="math inline">\(T(\cdot, \mathcal{X})\)</span> can be interpreted as an element of <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>. In other words, the data of a <span class="math inline">\((1,1)\)</span>-tensor, <span class="math inline">\(T : V^* \times V \xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R}\)</span>, is equivalent to the data of the linear map <span class="math inline">\(\varphi_T : V \xlongrightarrow{\sim} V\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-footnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-2"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-2" aria-label="Back to the text">2</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>The indices enclosed in parentheses, such as <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}^{(j)}\)</span>, refer strictly to the position of the argument within the tensor map <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span>. This is a purely positional convention used for clarity when expressing properties like multilinearity. Don’t confuse this with coordinate or basis indices.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-3"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-3" aria-label="Back to the text">3</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>We can equivalently write <span class="math inline">\(T \in T^{(r,s)} := \text{Hom}(\underbrace{V^* \times \dots \times V^*}_{r\text{-times}} \times \underbrace{V \times \dots \times V}_{s\text{-times}}, \mathbb{R})\)</span></p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>This identification holds because in finite-dimensional spaces, the double dual of any vector space is naturally isomorphic to the space itself. This is not generally true in infinite-dimensional settings, where the double dual can be strictly larger than the original space, unless additional conditions (like reflexivity) are satisfied.</p></div></div></div>

```
